etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English shortnen, schortenen, equivalent to short +‎ -en (verbal suffix). In some senses, a continuation (in altered form) of Middle English schorten (“to make short, shorten”), from Old English sċortian (“to become short”), from Proto-Germanic *skurtōną (“to shorten”).

quote.citation: [1877], Anna Sewell, “Earlshall”, in Black Beauty: […], London: Jarrold and Sons, […], →OCLC, part II, page 105:
quote.text: York came round to our heads and shortened the rein himself, one hole I think; every little makes a difference, be it for better or worse, and that day we had a steep hill to go up.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make deficient (as to); to deprive (of).

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “Aeneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Spoiled of his nose, and shorten'd of his ears.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To make short or friable, as pastry, with butter, lard, etc.
(transitive) To reduce or diminish in amount, quantity, or extent; to lessen.

quote.citation: 1699, John Dryden, Dedication to His Grace the Duke of Ormond:
quote.text: Here, where the subject is so fruitful, I am shortened by my chain.

quote.citation: 1858, George Borrow, The Romany Rye, volume 2, page 128:
quote.text: My grandfather, as I said before, was connected with a gang of shorters, and sometimes shortened money,  […]

definitions.definition: (baking, of pastries, transitive) To make crumbly.

quote.citation: 1894, Helen M. Laughlin, The Journal of Agriculture Cook Book, Journal of Agriculture Co., page 212:
quote.text: Corn flour makes delicious pie crust, and needs less lard to shorten it.

definitions.definition: (nautical, transitive) To take in the slack of (a rope).
(nautical, transitive) To reduce (sail) by taking it in.
